questions.question: Which finding provides the strongest evidence that a newborn is transferring enough milk?
choices: A combined pattern of swallowing, adequate output, satiety, and appropriate weight trajectory
Feeding for exactly ten minutes
Parent breast fullness alone
A newborn who never wakes to feed
questions.explanation: Adequacy is assessed through the whole dyad: effective swallowing, output, infant behavior, hydration, and weight—not duration or frequency alone.

questions.question: A five-day-old is difficult to wake, increasingly jaundiced, has few wet diapers, and continues losing weight. What is the best action?
choices: Recommend waiting one week
Assess only maternal nipple pain
Assume cluster feeding explains all findings
Arrange same-day pediatric evaluation of feeding, hydration, bilirubin, and weight
questions.explanation: Sleepiness, poor output, jaundice, and ongoing weight loss may indicate inadequate intake or illness and require prompt newborn assessment plus feeding support.

questions.question: Which approach is most appropriate for persistent nipple pain?
choices: Use aggressive nipple scrubbing
Stop all feeding without assessment
Assess latch, trauma, pump fit, dermatitis, vasospasm, infection, and infant function
Tell the patient pain is always normal
questions.explanation: Persistent pain has multiple possible causes. A focused parent-infant assessment guides treatment and protects feeding goals.

questions.question: Which advice is safest for inflammatory mastitis symptoms?
choices: Delay assessment despite fever and systemic illness
Use gentle physiologic milk removal and clinical assessment; avoid aggressive deep massage
Deeply knead the breast repeatedly
Stop all milk removal in every case
questions.explanation: Aggressive massage may worsen edema and tissue injury. Management should assess severity, support physiologic milk removal, and address bacterial infection or abscess when indicated.

questions.question: A breast mass persists after mastitis symptoms resolve. What should happen next?
choices: Prompt diagnostic breast evaluation, commonly beginning with ultrasound
Repeat antibiotics indefinitely without examination
Assume lactation makes cancer impossible
Wait until breastfeeding ends regardless of duration
questions.explanation: A persistent mass requires imaging and possible further evaluation. Lactation must not delay diagnosis of abscess, galactocele, or malignancy.

questions.question: What is the best principle for prescribing during lactation?
choices: Stop every essential maternal medicine
Assume all drugs enter milk at a dangerous level
Use only package labeling without clinical context
Use current drug-specific evidence and consider infant age, health, dose, route, and untreated maternal disease
questions.explanation: Lactation medication decisions are individualized. LactMed and other current evidence help balance infant exposure with the risk of untreated maternal illness.

questions.question: Which vitamin D plan generally applies to breastfed or partially breastfed newborns?
choices: Use an adult high-dose tablet for the infant
Rely on unprotected sun exposure
Provide 400 IU daily beginning in the first days unless an evidence-based alternative plan is made
No vitamin D is needed before age five
questions.explanation: Current CDC/AAP guidance supports 400 IU daily for breastfed and partially breastfed infants beginning shortly after birth, with careful product dosing.

questions.question: Which formula-safety instruction is essential?
choices: Use any unverified homemade recipe
Use the exact water-to-powder ratio and never dilute formula to extend supply
Add extra water whenever the infant is thirsty
Save unfinished room-temperature bottles all day
questions.explanation: Incorrect dilution can cause dangerous electrolyte and nutrition problems. Preparation, storage, water, and equipment instructions must be followed exactly.

questions.question: How should an FNP respond when a family chooses combination feeding?
choices: Provide nonjudgmental support for infant intake, milk supply goals, safe preparation, and sustainable follow-up
Refuse further lactation support
Assume the family lacks commitment
Hide formula-safety information
questions.explanation: Patient-centered feeding care supports informed goals and safety. Combination feeding may be appropriate and still benefits from skilled lactation and formula guidance.

questions.question: Which situation requires emergency rather than routine lactation follow-up?
choices: Questions about returning to work in two months
Mild breast fullness before a feed
A request to review pump-flange fit
A cyanotic, poorly arousable newborn with breathing difficulty
questions.explanation: Cyanosis, poor arousal, and respiratory distress are neonatal emergencies. Feeding assessment must never delay stabilization and emergency pediatric care.
